title: Prompting and Troubleshooting
description: Prompts that say what you want, strategies by task type, and fixing weak answers, limits and slow chats.

cards.definition: Say exactly what you want, including output format and constraints, and use numbered steps when order matters, instead of hoping Claude infers it.
Explain the purpose or audience behind an instruction, so Claude can tailor the answer to your goal and not just follow a bare rule.
A quick check: give your prompt to a coworker with no background on the task, and if they would be confused, Claude likely will be too.
A few sample inputs and outputs, ideally 3 to 5 that are relevant and varied, steer Claude's format, tone, and structure more reliably than description alone.
Wrapping instructions, context, examples, and inputs in separate descriptive tags helps Claude tell the parts of a long, mixed prompt apart.
Assigning Claude a role, even in one sentence, focuses its tone and behavior on your use case.
Splitting one big request into smaller parts so Claude handles each part well, instead of one sprawling ask.
Running the parts of a task as a sequence of prompts where each output feeds the next, such as draft, review, refine, so you can check each stage.
For research tasks, state what a good answer looks like and ask Claude to verify claims across several sources.
Replying in the same chat with clarifications or a rewrite request to refine an answer, rather than starting over.
When a first answer misses: rewrite the original prompt plainly, add background as if Claude knows nothing about you, and split big tasks.
When an answer is cut short, send your earlier prompt and Claude's reply back so it can pick up where it left off.
Controls how much reasoning Claude applies: higher gives more thorough answers but takes longer and uses limits faster, while low or medium suits routine tasks.
A separate control from effort that lets you view a summary of Claude's reasoning in an expandable section; availability depends on the model.
Latency and cost problems can sometimes be fixed more easily by choosing a different model than by rewriting the prompt.
A notice that Claude cannot respond right now because demand is high; it is not an outage, so wait a few minutes and try again.
A notice that your five-hour or weekly limit is used up; wait for the reset time, or continue on usage credits if they are enabled.
Documents in a Project's knowledge are cached, so reusing them counts less against limits, but the cache expires after inactivity and the first message afterward counts in full.
Combining related questions or tasks into one well-planned message with full context saves usage and avoids extra back-and-forth.
Disabling extended thinking, connectors, and web search when a chat does not need them reduces token use and stretches your usage limit.
Tell Claude what to do rather than what to avoid, for example asking for smoothly flowing prose paragraphs instead of saying no markdown.
Your prompt's own formatting influences the reply, so write it in the style you want back; removing markdown from the prompt reduces markdown in the output.
Newer models can default to longer answers, and effort settings do not reliably shorten them, so ask outright for brevity when you want a short draft.
For brainstorming or ambitious drafts, say you want more than the minimum, such as asking for as many relevant options as possible and going beyond the basics.
For complex research, ask Claude to form competing hypotheses, track its confidence, critique its own approach, and keep notes, so findings are transparent and checkable.
For analysis of long documents, place the documents at the top of the prompt and your question and instructions at the end, which can improve answer quality.
Opt-in pay-as-you-go balance for Pro and Max users: when a session or weekly limit is reached, requests continue at API rates instead of stopping.
